items.title: [ScienceDaily] Chang’e-6 lunar soil contains a surprising magnetic time capsule
items.content_html:
🌲 🏔️ ✏️

Scientists studying Chang’e-6 lunar soil have discovered a previously unknown magnetic mineral in natural Moon samples: a form of metallic iron called γ-Fe. Found inside tiny impact-glass particles, the nanoscale iron can preserve a stable magnetic signal, potentially acting like a microscopic fossil of the Moon’s long-lost magnetic field.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Powerful simulations reveal how the first stars changed the universe
items.content_html:
🌾 🔭 ✏️

Ultra-detailed simulations are showing how the first stars lit up the dark Universe and seeded space with elements such as carbon, oxygen, and iron. The MEGATRON project could bridge JWST observations of the earliest galaxies with chemical clues preserved in ancient stars today.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists just made a superconductor stronger using “empty space”
items.content_html:
🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Researchers have demonstrated that quantum fluctuations in supposedly empty space can strengthen superconductivity, raising the transition temperature of an ultrathin material by as much as 5.4%. The discovery opens the possibility of using specially engineered vacuum environments to control quantum materials without direct contact or external driving.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] NASA’s Roman telescope just opened its planet-hunting eye
items.content_html: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has demonstrated remarkable pointing stability and given its powerful planet-imaging coronagraph its first look at the cosmos. The telescope can already stay locked on a target with precision comparable to aiming a laser at a dime from about 150 miles away. Its coronagraph also captured stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, confirming that the instrument can produce focused images.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
items.content_html:
🌲 🏔️ ✏️

Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The early universe wasn’t nearly as pristine as scientists thought
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

JWST has revealed that galaxies were spreading carbon, oxygen, and other heavy elements through space just 500 million years after the Big Bang. The surprising discovery suggests the young universe became chemically enriched much earlier than expected, potentially erasing traces of its very first stars.

items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 ✏️

NASA’s Perseverance rover has uncovered a surprisingly complicated history of water in Jezero Crater. Scientists expected the crater’s Margin Unit to contain lake sediments, but instead found ancient igneous rocks that were altered by water on at least three separate occasions.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Black hole jets may decide the fate of entire galaxies
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 ✏️

Powerful jets from supermassive black holes can disturb star-forming gas far beyond a galaxy’s visible edge, leaving a glowing trail hundreds of thousands of light-years long. By keeping this gas hot and preventing it from falling inward, the jets may help determine whether a galaxy keeps forming stars or becomes quiet.

items.title: [news.google.com] Studies test Enceladus microbes and plume-particle chemistry
items.content_html: Two studies published in Science Advances examined whether a methane-producing Earth microorganism could remain active under laboratory conditions simulating Enceladus’s subsurface ocean, and how ocean material becomes ice grains in the moon’s plumes [scitechdaily.com#1][sciencedaily.com#1]. The microorganism survived, grew and produced methane in the simulated chemistry; the findings do not show that life exists on Enceladus [zmescience.com#1][newspaceeconomy.ca#1]. The second study found that ocean spray can sort and concentrate compounds into individual ice grains as it freezes and fragments. The process could also concentrate organic molecules and potential biosignatures [sciencedaily.com#1][astrobiology.com#1][scitechdaily.com#1].

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] America gets a chatbot
items.content_html:
The federal government has a chatbot.

President Donald Trump launched america.gov on Tuesday, a new site that looks like ChatGPT or Claude with a prompt box to query the federal government. The underlying LLM draws its responses from official state sources.

“With america.gov, the federal government no longer stands in your way, and it stands only at your service, and that’s what we’re doing,” Trump said at the unveiling. “We’re simplifying it, we’re glamorizing it, we’re making it what it should be.”

Trump signed an executive order Tuesday establishing the site, and according to the executive order, it excludes tax filing services provided by the Internal Revenue Service as well as services provided by the intelligence community and the Defense Department.

The site features a prompt box under a welcome message that reads, “Hello, America” and “Whatever you need from government, start here.” Suggested prompts include “How do I register my new business?,” “How do I replace my Social Security card?,” and “How do I book a campsite in a national park?”

The idea is that citizens can simply ask the chatbot for answers instead of navigating digital government bureaucracy online. The site says by next year people will be able to use it to enroll in Medicare, apply for a passport, find a federal government job, and more. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

“You’ll now have one front door for every single question,” Trump said. “Everything will be answered easily and quickly.”

The National Design Studio, Trump’s government design office staffed by former DOGE staffers and headed by Airbnb cofounder and Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia, designed the website. Like other sites the the studio has worked on—Realfood.gov and TrumpRX.gov, for example—the chatbot site is designed with a consumer sheen, with information laid out like an Apple product page in graphics inside squares with rounded corners. America.gov represents the office’s most ambitious rollout yet.

In an introductory message on the homepage that says in part that the site “uses AI to get simple answers only from official government sources,” in-line images and symbols are used like glyphs, a trend called Nouveau Rebus. The symbols are interactive. Click an arrow icon and it turns into a U.S. flag. Tap a trio of federal government seals and it shuffles into different agencies.

For all its gloss, America.gov is powered by an LMM, and comes amid rising public adoption of and worries over AI, including in government. A recent move to automate U.S. Web Design System accessibility testing has experts concerned it will hurt progress in making federal sites more accessible.

The website’s frequently asked questions page notes that “AI can make mistakes, so check the sources included with each answer before making an important decision.” There’s a feedback button to report a problem.

The FAQ also says the site doesn’t provide campaign or party information and “answers are based on published government sources.” The chatbot correctly identifies former President Joe Biden as the winner of the 2020 election, for example, instead of parroting Trump’s false claims. Using official government sources is great in theory for getting accurate, neutral government information from the source, but since this administration deletes government sites and scrubs information it doesn’t like, it also raises concerns about the potential to manipulate it.

America.gov doesn’t require a login to use, and according to its privacy policy, the site claims it collects no personal information, tracks no analytics nor locations, and keeps no conversations. A Guardian investigation this summer found National Design Studio has run commercial visitor-tracking software on sites that didn’t meet federal privacy standards.

While the website represents an innovation in digital government services, it’s part of a wider AI boom that’s seeing chatbots stuffed everywhere, and part of a larger bet that prompt boxes and AI responses are increasingly the way people interface with information today.

Pew Research Center found the percentage of U.S. adults who use AI is up from a third to nearly half since 2024. Even still, 71% believe the increased use of AI will make their personal information less secure, while 40% believe AI will have a negative impact on society over the next 20 years compared to just 16% who believe it will be positive.

Bringing government services into the AI age is a tall order ripe with challenges, but a successful chatbot could prove what’s possible. The federal government’s newest website represents a major public-facing test.
